pages.x: Greek tradition says the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus in the west of the Peloponnese. There was one event, a sprint of one stadion, about 192 metres, and the first winner on record was a cook named Koroibos, from the nearby town of Elis.

Every four years heralds announced a truce, so athletes and crowds could travel safely to Olympia from all over the Greek world. The four-year cycle, an Olympiad, became a way of counting time, and the list of winners gives some of the first fixed dates in Greek history.

In time the festival grew to five days, with longer races, wrestling, boxing, chariot races and the pentathlon. Athletes competed naked and rubbed with olive oil. Married women were not allowed to watch, though unmarried girls ran their own races in honour of the goddess Hera.

The only prize at Olympia was a wreath cut from a sacred olive tree, though home towns gave winners free meals for life and statues. Cheats were fined, and the fines paid for bronze statues of Zeus that lined the way into the stadium, each with a cheat's name on its base.

The most famous champion was the wrestler Milo of Croton, who won six times in the 500s BC. Legend says he grew strong by carrying a newborn calf on his shoulders every day until it was a full-grown bull.

pages.t: The end, and a new start
pages.x: The games went on for more than a thousand years, until the 390s AD, when the Christian emperor Theodosius banned pagan festivals. In 1896 a French baron, Pierre de Coubertin, revived them in Athens, and they have been held every four years since, except during the world wars.

The ancient games gave the quarrelsome Greek cities a festival they shared, and gave the world the idea of sport as a peaceful contest between peoples. The Olympic flame for today's games is still lit at Olympia.
pts: Held every four years under a sacred truce
